job/job: A language model reads text and predicts what comes next. Take the text cats like fresh fish daily.
job/shift: After cats comes like. After cats like comes fresh. The targets are the text itself, shifted by one.
job/once: A recurrent network worked through this one step at a time. This model makes all four predictions at once, in a single pass.
job/peek: But at once, the answers sit right there in the input. Position one, reading like, could simply look ahead at fresh and copy it.
job/causal: So each position may see only itself and what came before. That rule is called causal, as in cause and effect: a later token can never change what an earlier position says.
job/decoder: The Transformer, in 2017, was built for translation, with an encoder and a decoder like the recurrent ones before it. The encoder read the source sentence, and the decoder wrote the translation one token at a time, under exactly this rule.
job/only: A language model has no source sentence to read, so it keeps only the decoder. In 2018, Peter Liu and colleagues used such a decoder-only model to write Wikipedia articles.
job/gpt: That same year, Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI trained one on over seven thousand unpublished books. It came to be called GPT, for generative pre-trained transformer: a transformer, trained on plain text, that generates more of it.
stack/ids: Now build it, from the bottom up. The four tokens come in as ids: a list of T numbers, and here T is four.
stack/embed: Each id becomes its row of the embedding table, E. That gives x: T vectors of d numbers, T by d.
stack/pos: Attention cannot tell where a token sits, so each position adds a learned vector of its own. The shape stays T by d.
stack/blocks: Then come N transformer blocks, one after another. Each takes T by d and hands back T by d, so they stack.
stack/causal: In every block, attention is causal: the mask hides every later position. Position two looks back at zero and one, and at itself, but never ahead at three.
stack/why: So no position can see the token it must predict, and all T positions still run at once.
out/unembed: At the top, the unembedding scores every vocabulary token at every position: T by d becomes T by V.
out/softmax: A softmax on each row turns its scores into probabilities for the next token.
out/shift: Row zero has read only cats, and puts the most on like. Row one puts it on fresh, and row two on fish.
out/last: Row three has read all four, so it predicts the token after fish: here, daily. At the end of a text, that last row is the next word to write.
out/count: So T tokens in give T predictions out, all from one pass through the model. A batch of B texts gives B times T.
out/loss: Every prediction has a target, so every one gets a cross-entropy loss. Training adds up all four: four lessons from a single pass.
